source_text: Quod porro Anima sit substantia, sic ostenditur: Primo quidem, quoniam illi quoque definitio substantiae iure convenit, quae quidem est eiusmodi: Substantia est id, quod cum unum et idem sit numero, contraria vicissim suscipit. Quod vero Anima a natura propria non recedens, contraria vicissim suscipiat, omnibus credo est perspicuum. Iustitia enim et iniustitia, fortitudo et timiditas, temperantia et intemperantia, in ipsa vicissim cernuntur, quum sint contraria. Quamobrem cum ea substantiae sit proprietas, ut contrariorum vicissim susceptrix sit, eademque Animae conveniat; substantia igitur anima erit. Praeterea, cum et corpus sit substantia, Animam quoque substantiam esse necesse est. Neque enim fieri potest, ut quod vitam accipit, substantia sit; illud autem quod vitam praebet, non sit substantia. Nisi forte quis ita insaniat, ut id quod non est, eius quod est, causam esse affirmet: aut rursus id, cuius illud ipsum quod est, ex alio sic pendet, ut absque illo esse nequeat, eius, ipsius, ex quo pendet, causam esse velit.
orientation: Gregory continues his treatise addressed to Tatian, now demonstrating by philosophical reasoning that the soul is a substance rather than an accident, using the definition of substance as that which remains numerically one while receiving contraries.
pass_a_gloss: Furthermore, that the Soul is a substance, is shown thus: First indeed, because that definition of substance fits it also justly, which definition is of this sort: Substance is that which, while it is one and the same in number, receives contraries in turn. That however the Soul, not departing from its own nature, receives contraries in turn, is clear to all, I believe. For justice and injustice, courage and timidity, temperance and intemperance, are discerned in it in turn, since they are contraries. Wherefore since it is a property of substance to be a receiver of contraries in turn, and this same thing agrees with the Soul; therefore the Soul will be a substance. Moreover, since even the body is a substance, it is necessary that the Soul also be a substance. For it is not possible that what receives life is a substance; but that which supplies life is not a substance. Unless perhaps someone so rages as to affirm that what is not is the cause of that which is: or again that which depends on another for its very being, so that without that other it cannot be, he wishes that very thing on which it depends to be the cause of it.

choices.english: Furthermore, that the Soul is a substance
choices.why: Standard logical transition; 'porro' marks the next major step in the argument.
rejected: But that the Soul is a substance
Moreover, the Soul being a substance

choices.english: that definition of substance fits it justly
choices.why: 'Iure' = justly, rightly, by right; the definition applies properly to the soul.
rejected: the definition of substance suits it legally
the definition of substance agrees with it by law

choices.why: 'Vicissim' means alternately, in succession; the soul undergoes contrary states one after another while remaining numerically one.

choices.english: not departing from its own nature
choices.why: The soul receives contraries without ceasing to be what it is; this is essential to the Aristotelian definition of substance.
rejected: not deviating from its proper nature

choices.why: Strong rhetorical term: to assert that a non-being causes a being, or that the dependent is cause of that on which it depends, is madness.
Causal language: the argument moves from ontological priority (substance) to causal priority (life-giver).

pass_b_english: Furthermore, that the soul is a substance is shown as follows. First, the definition of substance fits it justly. That definition is this: Substance is that which, while remaining numerically one and the same, receives contraries in turn. That the soul, without departing from its own nature, receives contraries in turn, I believe is clear to everyone. For justice and injustice, courage and cowardice, temperance and intemperance are perceived in the soul in turn, since they are contraries. Therefore, since it is a property of substance to be the recipient of contraries in turn, and this same property belongs to the soul, the soul is therefore a substance. Moreover, since the body is a substance, the soul must also be a substance. For it is not possible that what receives life is a substance, while what supplies life is not a substance. Unless someone is so insane as to affirm that what does not exist is the cause of what does exist, or again to claim that a thing whose very existence so depends on another that it cannot exist without it is the cause of that very thing on which it depends.

problems.quote: the thing on which that which exists depends in such a way that it cannot exist without it is itself the cause of that on which it depends
problems.source_quote: id, cuius illud ipsum quod est, ex alio sic pendet, ut absque illo esse nequeat, eius, ipsius, ex quo pendet, causam esse velit
problems.why: The dependency is reversed and garbled. In the Latin, the dependent thing (whose existence hangs on another) is said to cause the thing it depends on. The English makes the dependee the subject.
problems.fix: or, again, to claim that a thing whose very existence so depends on another that it cannot exist without it is the cause of that very thing on which it depends.

edits.old: Unless someone is so insane as to affirm that what does not exist is the cause of what does exist, or again to claim that the thing on which that which exists depends in such a way that it cannot exist without it is itself the cause of that on which it depends.
edits.new: Unless someone is so insane as to affirm that what does not exist is the cause of what does exist, or again to claim that a thing whose very existence so depends on another that it cannot exist without it is the cause of that very thing on which it depends.

fixed: Fixed reversed dependency in the final clause: the Latin says the dependent thing (id, cuius illud ipsum quod est, ex alio sic pendet) is claimed to be the cause of that on which it depends (eius, ipsius, ex quo pendet). The edit makes the dependent thing the subject ('a thing whose very existence so depends on another... is the cause of that very thing on which it depends').
